item.research_question: How does the addition of Zirconium (Zr) affect the phase stability, microstructure evolution, and mechanical (hardness, compressive strength, creep) and corrosion properties of cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys?
item.material_system: ZrxAlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy alloys with x = 0, 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting (cold crucible floating melting) under argon protection; each alloy remelted at least five times; cast ingot diameter 44 mm
item.test_conditions: Microhardness: 0.981 N load, 15 s dwell; Compression: room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1, strain 0.3; Nanoindentation creep: peak load 10 mN, hold 100 s, loading rates 0.1, 1, and 5 mN/s; Corrosion: 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, EIS 10−2 to 104 Hz, cyclic polarization −0.8 V to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s
key_findings: At x = 0.05, the alloy reached peak hardness of 368.1 HV, an increase of approximately 18.7% compared to the Zr-free alloy.
At x = 0.05, the compressive strength reached 1801.1 MPa, an increase of approximately 52.2% compared to the Zr-free alloy.
At x = 0.05, the yield strength reached 1048.7 MPa, an increase of approximately 48.7% compared to the Zr-free alloy.
At x = 0.1, the alloy exhibited the lowest self-corrosion current density of 0.034197 μA/cm2 and the highest pitting potential of 323.06 mV.
At a loading rate of 0.1 mN/s, the creep stress exponent n exceeded 3 for all Zr contents, indicating dislocation creep as the dominant mechanism.
At x = 0.1, the microstructure transitioned from a discontinuous to a continuous network of Ni7Zr2 precipitates at phase boundaries.
At x = 0.1, the compressive strength decreased to 1382.4 MPa, a reduction of 418.7 MPa compared to the x = 0.05 alloy.
The addition of Zr promoted the formation of Ni7Zr2 intermetallic compounds which acted as a bridge between the FCC and B2 phases.
item.mechanism: Zr addition enhances performance through solid-solution strengthening (lattice distortion) and precipitation strengthening (formation of Ni7Zr2). At optimal content (x=0.05), these mechanisms maximize strength and creep resistance by hindering grain boundary sliding and dislocation motion. At high content (x=0.1), excessive formation of continuous Ni7Zr2 networks and Ni precipitation from the B2 phase lead to phase coarsening, depletion of strengthening elements, and embrittlement, reducing mechanical properties but improving corrosion resistance via a stable, dense oxide film.
item.limitations: The text states that 'excessive Zr segregation can result in embrittlement, particularly with the development of a continuous network of Zr-rich phases and zirconides' and that at x=0.1, 'excessive strengthening, grain boundary pinning, restricted dislocation motion, and embrittlement owing to phase transformation' occur, leading to reduced mechanical properties.
item.future_work: The authors state that 'Further research on the mechanical properties will provide deeper insights into the performance variations with different Zr contents' and that the study provides a 'theoretical foundation for designing room-temperature creep-resistant materials, particularly for structural applications under low loading rates.'
quotes: At x = 0.05, the creep exponent exceeded 3, indicating that dislocation creep mechanisms dominated.
The addition of Zr significantly affected the phase stability, promoting the formation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Zr2, which acted as a bridge between the FCC and B2 phases.
